An inverse bind pose matrix is the inverse of a bone's global transform in the [[Bind Pose]]. It converts an object-space bind vertex into that bone's local coordinate space.

Multiplying this matrix by the bone's current global pose creates a skinning transform. Without the inverse bind step, applying the animated bone transform would incorrectly include the original bind placement twice.

An inverse function reverses a one-to-one function: $f^{-1}(f(x))=x$ on the original domain. Its graph is the reflection of the original graph across $y=x$, and its domain and range are exchanged. A function must assign distinct outputs to distinct inputs, or its domain must be restricted before an inverse can be defined.

An inverse of a square matrix $A$ is a matrix $A^{-1}$ satisfying $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$. It exists only when $A$ is a [[Nonsingular Matrix]], equivalently when its [[Determinant]] is nonzero.

For a system $Ax=b$, multiplication by the inverse gives $x=A^{-1}b$. In computation, a direct solver or [[LU Decomposition]] is usually preferable to explicitly forming the inverse.

The closed-form least-squares expression includes the inverse of the design cross-product, but the source cautions that explicitly computing it with `solve` can be numerically unstable. A [[QR Decomposition]] is preferred for fitting in practical software.

The primer expresses formal finite element solutions through an inverse of the reduced global matrix. For large assembled systems, solving the equations directly is preferable to explicitly constructing that inverse.

An inverse-square law has the form $y=k/x^2$. Doubling the distance variable reduces the dependent quantity to one quarter. Plotting $y$ against $1/x^2$ produces a straight line through the origin when the relationship holds. Such laws commonly arise when a conserved influence spreads across spherical area proportional to $x^2$.

An invisible function return provides a value without automatically printing it at the console. It suits functions whose main visible effect is a plot or message while still allowing assignment of a useful result.

The hidden display behavior should be documented because the value remains available to callers.

An IP subnet mask identifies which bits of an IPv4 address describe the network and which describe the host within that network. Applying the mask lets a device determine whether a destination is local or must be reached through a router.

Variable-length subnet masking allows the boundary to use an arbitrary prefix length instead of being fixed by the older address classes. That flexibility supports differently sized subnets within the available address space.

An IPv4 address is a 32-bit identifier used to address an interface on an Internet Protocol network. It is commonly written as four decimal octets separated by periods.

The limited address space led to address-sharing techniques and motivated [[IPv6 Address|IPv6]]. A game normally relies on networking APIs and name resolution rather than embedding numeric addresses directly.

An IPv6 address is a 128-bit Internet Protocol address, conventionally written as hexadecimal groups separated by colons. The much larger address space addresses the exhaustion limits of [[IPv4 Address|IPv4]].

Networked games should use address-family-neutral APIs when possible so endpoint handling does not assume one textual format or address size.

An irrational number is a real number that cannot be expressed as a quotient of two [[Integer]]s. Its decimal expansion is infinite and nonrepeating.

For example, (sqrt{2}) is irrational, so any finite calculator display of it is an approximation rather than an exact equality. The same distinction applies to (pi): values such as (3.14) or (22/7) can be close, but they are not equal to it. Rational and irrational numbers together form the [[Real Number]]s.

An irreducible ideal is an [[Ideal]] I that cannot be written as I = I₁ ∩ I₂ with both I₁ and I₂ strictly larger than I. Any such intersection forces one component to equal I.

In a [[Noetherian Ring]], every ideal is a finite intersection of irreducible ideals. The source uses this finiteness as a step toward [[Primary Decomposition of Ideals]].

An irreducible polynomial is a nonconstant polynomial that cannot be factored into nonconstant polynomials of smaller degree over the chosen coefficient ring or field.

Over a [[Field]], an irreducible polynomial that divides a product divides at least one factor. This prime-like behavior supports the [[Unique Factorization of Polynomials]]. Irreducibility always depends on the coefficient domain.

The source connects irreducibility to maximal principal ideals in K[x]. Quotienting by the ideal generated by an irreducible polynomial produces a field in which the coset of x acts as a root.

An irregular space-time layout contains measured position-time pairs with no shared grid or obvious repeated organization. Locations, times, or both may differ from one observation to the next. STI and [[STIDF Object|STIDF]] represent this form in the `spacetime` package. Analysis and visualization cannot assume a complete array, so observations must be selected or aggregated through their explicit coordinates and time indexes.

An isometric tile map arranges diamond-shaped tiles so a two-dimensional image suggests a three-dimensional angled view. Grid coordinates must be transformed into slanted screen coordinates rather than mapped directly to horizontal and vertical pixels.

The underlying level can still use a regular tile grid, but rendering order and coordinate conversion must preserve the apparent depth relationship among tiles and objects.

An isoparametric quadrilateral element uses the same shape functions to map element geometry and interpolate field variables. Natural coordinates describe a regular parent element that is transformed into the physical quadrilateral.

Higher-order versions add side nodes and can represent curved boundaries. The mapping lets a common formulation handle a range of element shapes while numerical integration evaluates transformed coefficients.

An isotropic material uses the same thermal conductivity in every direction. An anisotropic material requires directional values, so conductive heat flux need not align simply with a scalar conductivity times the temperature gradient.

Transversely isotropic materials share properties within a plane but differ normal to it, while orthotropic materials have three distinct values along orthogonal axes. Rolled sheet and layered structures therefore require orientation-aware inputs in [[Finite Element Thermal Modeling|finite-element models]].

An IT department acting as a cloud service broker curates available services, negotiates or oversees provider relationships, integrates capabilities, and helps business units choose approved offerings. Its focus moves from owning every system to governing a service portfolio.

This role can give departments more autonomy while retaining shared standards for security, interoperability, reporting, and continuity. The catalog must respond to real needs or users may create [[Shadow IT]] outside the broker's view.

An itemset is a finite set of items considered together in a transaction database. Its occurrence is counted in every transaction containing all of its members.

Frequent itemsets provide the candidates from which association rules are derived. The number of possible itemsets grows exponentially with the number of distinct items.

An iteration control structure repeats a sequence of steps while a continuation condition holds or until a stopping condition is reached. It is also called a loop.

Iteration lets an [[Algorithm]] apply the same operation to successive data or progressively improve a result. Its condition must support [[Algorithm Termination]]; otherwise the procedure can enter an infinite loop and fail to produce its intended output.

An iteration matrix expresses a linear update as $x^{(k+1)}=Tx^{(k)}+c$. The error after successive steps is controlled by powers of $T$.

A stationary iteration converges for every starting vector when the [[Spectral Radius]] of $T$ is less than one. Matrix norms can provide easier sufficient tests.

An iterative classification algorithm for networks alternates between predicting node labels and rebuilding relational features from the current predictions of neighboring nodes. Initial labels usually come from a classifier using only local attributes.

Iteration lets mutually dependent predictions reinforce one another until a stopping condition is reached. It can also amplify an early mistake, so confidence controls, update ordering, and convergence behavior matter.

An iterative convergence criterion determines when an approximation process should stop or whether it will approach the desired solution. A practical rule compares successive approximations or the residual against a chosen tolerance.

A theoretical criterion may use the [[Spectral Radius]] or a norm of the [[Iteration Matrix]]. Small step-to-step change should be interpreted with care because it does not always guarantee a small solution error.

An iterative linear solver begins with an approximate vector and repeatedly applies an update intended to approach the solution of $Ax=b$. It produces usable approximations before exact arithmetic would finish.

These methods are attractive for large [[Sparse Matrix|sparse matrices]], where direct elimination may require excessive work or destroy sparsity. Convergence depends on the coefficient matrix and the chosen iteration.

An LDLT factorization writes a symmetric matrix as $A=LDL^T$, where $L$ is unit lower triangular and $D$ is diagonal.

It separates diagonal scaling from triangular structure and avoids square roots required by [[Cholesky Decomposition]]. The form is useful when symmetry is available even when the matrix is not positive definite.

An LSTM forget gate decides how much of the previous [[LSTM Cell State|cell state]] to retain at a new sequence step. It processes the current input together with the prior hidden output using sigmoid units, producing a vector of values between zero and one.

Multiplying the old cell state elementwise by this vector suppresses entries with gate values near zero and retains entries with values near one. The gate's role is selective memory removal, distinct from adding new information through the [[LSTM Input Gate]] or deciding what to reveal through the [[LSTM Output Gate]].

An LSTM output gate selects which parts of the updated [[LSTM Cell State|cell state]] become the hidden output at the current time step. The cell state is passed through tanh to form a candidate output; a sigmoid gate, computed from the current input and prior hidden output, filters that candidate element by element.

The resulting vector is sent toward the network's output and is also carried as the next step's hidden context. This is different from the [[LSTM Forget Gate]], which filters stored memory, and the [[LSTM Input Gate]], which adds selected information to it.

An m-adic prefix tree branches according to successive digits in base m. In a decimal tree, the first digit chooses one of ten root bins, the second digit divides each bin again, and deeper levels represent finer precision.

Each record can be placed by reading its code from left to right. The resulting hierarchy is simultaneously a set of nested cluster bins and an index for matching or retrieval. It need not be a prime-base p-adic number system; the book uses m-adic to include practical nonprime bases such as decimal.

An MHD topping cycle extracts electrical power while combustion gas is still very hot and conducting, then sends its remaining heat to a steam or gas-turbine bottoming plant. Conductivity drops as gas cools, so extending the MHD channel alone cannot use all of its thermal energy. Combining stages uses a wider temperature range and raises total fuel utilization over either stage alone.

An ML.NET learning pipeline chains estimators that prepare columns and train an algorithm. Fitting the pipeline against training data produces a transformer capable of applying the learned sequence to compatible input data.

Keeping preparation and learning in one pipeline ensures the same transformations are applied during training and prediction. The fitted pipeline can be saved as a model artifact together with the input schema required to load it later.

An MVC controller is a server-side class whose action methods handle routed requests. A controller does not have to render an HTML view: in a Web API it can return structured data such as JSON for a browser client.

Controllers sit behind the [[HTTP Request Pipeline]] and are reached through [[Endpoint Routing]]. This lets an Angular [[Single-Page Application]] request data without moving server-side presentation logic into the client.

An n-boundary is an element in the image of the differential dₙ₊₁: Cₙ₊₁ → Cₙ. It is produced by applying the preceding map in a [[Chain Complex]].

Since dₙdₙ₊₁ = 0, every boundary lies in the kernel of dₙ and is therefore a [[Cycle in a Chain Complex]]. Homology identifies cycles that differ by a boundary.

An n-cycle is an element of the kernel of the differential dₙ: Cₙ → Cₙ₋₁. It is sent to zero by the next map in a [[Chain Complex]].

Every [[Boundary in a Chain Complex]] is a cycle, but a cycle need not be a boundary. The quotient of cycles by boundaries is the n-th [[Homology Group]].

An n-gram language model estimates the probability of a word from a fixed number of preceding words. Counts in a text corpus provide probabilities for recurring sequences such as unigrams, bigrams, or trigrams.

Its limited history makes computation manageable during [[Speech Recognition Search]], but it cannot directly preserve distant context. Smoothing is needed when a plausible sequence was rare or absent in the training text.

An n-type semiconductor has donor impurity levels close to the conduction band. Electrons can be promoted from these levels into available conduction states at ordinary temperatures, making electrons its main mobile carriers. Paired with a [[P-Type Semiconductor]], it forms a [[P-N Junction]] whose field can separate light-generated carriers. The impurity amount affects conductivity.

An OAuth client is the application requesting an access token so it can call a protected resource. IdentityServer configuration identifies the client, its allowed grant, credentials, and the scopes or API resources it may request.

In the stock checker, the UWP application is the client and the ASP.NET Core API is the resource. Defining the client in the authorization server makes its permitted path to a token an explicit part of the system's trust model.

An OAuth grant type defines the interaction through which a client obtains authorization and an access token. It identifies which participant supplies credentials, what trust the client receives, and whether user interaction occurs at the authorization server.

Grant selection is a security and usability decision rather than a interchangeable configuration label. The book examines the limitations of its [[Resource Owner Password Grant]] and notes that a server-hosted login can keep sensitive authentication logic out of desktop code.

An OAuth resource is the protected service for which an access token is intended. The stock-checker API is registered as a resource, and its authentication middleware treats the IdentityServer authority as the issuer whose tokens it will validate.

A token meant for one resource should not be treated as general permission across every service. Resource configuration gives the authorization server and API a shared name for the boundary being protected.

An OAuth scope names a permission or access boundary a client may request for a resource. Scopes help limit a token to the part of a service the client actually needs rather than granting undifferentiated authority.

The book's IdentityServer configuration associates its client with the protected API scope before requesting a token. Application-specific role checks can further narrow individual operations after the token has established access to the resource.

An object is in free fall when gravity is the only significant force acting on it. Near Earth's surface and over modest height changes, its acceleration is approximately constant and downward, independent of mass when air resistance is neglected. Apparent weightlessness in orbit is continuous free fall rather than absence of gravity.

An objective function assigns a value to each candidate solution in an optimization problem. The task is to find a permitted point that minimizes or maximizes this value.

In [[Linear Programming]], the objective is linear. In [[Nonlinear Programming]], either the objective or at least one constraint is nonlinear. The objective must be interpreted together with the [[Feasible Solution|feasible solutions]] defined by the constraints.

An oblique Mercator reorients the cylinder so the line of tangency follows a selected great-circle corridor rather than the Equator or a meridian. Distortion is minimized along that oblique reference, allowing a long route to be represented inside the chart's useful band. The method is a projection equivalent of rotating coordinates to fit the path of interest.

An observable mobile repository exposes a stream of data results rather than returning only one final collection. It can publish a cached local result immediately and later publish a refreshed remote result, allowing the view model to react without coordinating both stores directly.

This arrangement separates storage selection from presentation logic. Subscribers still need clear rules for ordering, completion, errors, and whether a later result replaces or merges with the earlier value.

An observable represents a sequence of values or events that a consumer can subscribe to over time. It fits asynchronous client behavior because the producer can emit a result, an error, or later updates without blocking the caller.

Angular [[Angular HttpClient|HttpClient]] returns observables for HTTP operations. Components and services can transform, retry, or react to those streams, and an activity log can observe form changes without repeatedly polling the form model.

.NET's `IObservable<T>` expresses the producer side of the same general idea: an observer subscribes, receives notifications as values change, and can dispose of the subscription. The inventory example makes a product recorder the provider for several reporting observers, keeping the provider independent of each report's behavior.

An observation model gives the probability of a measurement conditioned on a hidden state. It expresses how an inaccessible state is expected to appear through an imperfect sensor or other evidence source.

During filtering, this likelihood reweights the predicted state distribution. An informative observation concentrates belief on states that could plausibly have produced the measured value.

An odds ratio compares the odds of a binary outcome between a focal predictor state and its reference. It equals the exponential of a logistic regression coefficient when the predictor changes by one unit.

An odds ratio of one indicates equal odds, values above one indicate higher odds, and values below one indicate lower odds. Odds are not probabilities or risk ratios, so the distinction becomes important when the outcome is common.

An odds ratio confidence interval exponentiates the lower and upper confidence limits of a logistic coefficient. It communicates both the plausible magnitude of the association and the precision of the estimate on the odds-ratio scale.

An interval that includes one does not support a nonzero association at the corresponding two-sided level. Reporting the interval is generally more informative than reporting only a p-value because it shows which effect sizes remain compatible with the model.

An offsite backup stores a recovery copy in a location separated from the primary system. A fire, theft, electrical event, or local configuration error can then damage the original environment without necessarily destroying its backup.

A cloud backup service can supply this geographic separation. Sensitive data should be protected before or during transfer, and the restoration path must remain available when the primary site is not.

An omnidirectional light probe records the incident illumination around a point, supplying both a record of a location and a possible image-based-lighting source. The book distinguishes a high-dynamic-range probe from an ordinary spherical lighting reference that captures similar directions without the same intensity range. Bracketed exposures can be merged to extend that range. Even a regular blurred environment image may provide useful soft fill, often combined with a separate sun or key light. The goal is a match to the photographed set, not merely a technically elaborate lighting rig. See [[Plate Lighting Reference for CG]].

An ongoing responsibility register identifies work that must recur throughout development rather than finish once, such as maintaining builds, updating documentation, organizing tests, or checking asset integration. It names an owner without reducing the responsibility to a single checkbox.

Separating recurring duties from ordinary tasks prevents essential maintenance from disappearing each time the immediate task list is reprioritized.

An online algorithm processes input incrementally rather than requiring the complete problem instance before it begins. At every point it maintains a solution based on the information received so far.

This property is useful when data arrive as a stream or future input is unknown. [[Insertion Sort]] can maintain an ordered collection as new items arrive, while a greedy edge-coloring procedure can schedule matches even when contestants join after scheduling has begun.

An online game is a multiplayer distributed game whose participants' machines communicate over a network. Online describes the connection arrangement rather than a particular genre.

Separate screens allow private information and individual viewpoints, but the design must handle transmission delay, arrival, departure, failure, security, communication, and the social consequences of remote play.

An ontology is an explicit organization of concepts, properties, and relationships in a domain. For language understanding, it provides a shared structure into which phrases can be mapped.

An [[Intent Schema]] is a practical, task-oriented form of conceptual organization. Rich ontologies can support inference, but creating and maintaining them is labor-intensive and limits the easy scaling of hand-built understanding systems.

has moved each FixedUpdate, and if the Projectile has moved less than 0.01m for ten
consecutive frames, we'll decide to treat it as if it's asleep.

An open endpoint is a boundary value excluded from an [[Interval]]. It corresponds to a strict inequality such as (x<2) or (x>-1).

On a [[Number Line]], exclusion is shown with an unfilled circle at the boundary. In interval notation, a parenthesis is used. Values may approach the endpoint arbitrarily closely while the endpoint itself remains outside the set. This differs from a [[Closed Endpoint]], which is included through an equality option.

An open level layout gives the player largely unconstrained movement across a broad space. Obstacles and restricted regions may exist, but the player is not forced through one dominant route.

Open layouts support exploration and strategic positioning while making sequence and pacing harder to control. Landmarks, goals, terrain, and information must help players choose direction without requiring a fixed path.

An open nested transaction can expose its committed effects before the parent transaction finishes. This improves concurrency because other work need not wait for the entire parent.

Early visibility weakens simple rollback: if the parent later aborts, the system may need a compensating action rather than erasing an effect that other transactions have already observed.

An open prompt invites a wide range of user requests, as in asking how the assistant can help. It gives the user initiative but provides little linguistic constraint to recognition and understanding.

After an open prompt, the system must perform broad [[Intent Triggering]] and [[Candidate Hypothesis Ranking]]. If confidence is low, it can narrow the interaction with a [[Directed Prompt]].

An open story is an emergent narrative with relatively few controlled outcomes and substantial room for players to create their own experiences. The creator facilitates a space in which stories can arise rather than determining which story must be delivered.

Open stories trade authorial control for variety and unpredictability. They may emerge from complex systems, player-created goals, shared authorship, or multiplayer interaction, and they need not resemble a polished traditional plot to be worth retelling.

An open-cycle MHD system burns fuel to make a hot gas stream, adds an ionizing seed, accelerates the gas through a nozzle, and extracts direct current in an [[MHD Generator Duct]]. Exhaust heat preheats incoming oxidant; seed recovery and pollution control precede discharge. Unlike a [[Closed-Cycle MHD System]], the working gas is not continuously recirculated through the same loop.

An open-source game engine exposes its source and grants reuse under its license, but engines still differ in editor workflow, scripting language, renderer, platform support, asset formats, and integration with Blender.

Selection should follow project needs and the team's ability to validate the complete asset path. Godot emphasizes a standalone node-based editor, Stride offers a modular C# toolchain, and Armory3D integrates game production more directly into Blender.

An OpenGL context is the stateful environment that owns rendering configuration and GPU objects for a window. It must be created and made current before OpenGL functions can initialize buffers, shaders, textures, or draw commands.

Resources belong to a context or an explicitly shared context group. The engine therefore creates graphics resources after context initialization and destroys them before the context and window are released.

An OpenGL framebuffer object groups color, depth, or stencil attachments that receive rendering output. Attachments can be textures or renderbuffers with dimensions and formats compatible with the intended pass.

After construction, framebuffer completeness must be checked before drawing. Binding the object enables [[Render to Texture]], while rebinding the default framebuffer returns output to the window.

An operational level agreement states the service commitment between an internal supplier and an internal consumer in the same organization. For example, an IT department can agree with a business department on the availability and delivery of an internal computing service.

It resembles a [[Service Level Agreement]] but applies within the organizational boundary. When an internal service depends on an external provider, its operational objectives should be compatible with the external commitment it receives.

An operator combines with one or more operands to produce or assign a value. Unary operators act on one operand, such as negation or increment, while binary operators combine two operands, such as addition, comparison, or multiplication.

The same symbol can behave differently for different operand types because types define which operations they support. Parentheses and precedence determine grouping, so explicit grouping is valuable when a compact expression could be read in more than one way.

An operator registration function fills a [[Blender Operator Type Structure]] with identity, description, flags, properties, and function pointers. For the icosphere example, the registration assigns a concrete execution function to `exec` and a context-checking function to `poll`.

This binding separates the persistent description of an operation from the code that performs it. A later user event retrieves the registered type, the [[Blender Operator Poll Method]] decides whether it is valid in the current context, and the execution callback changes Blender data.

An operator's `exec` callback performs the actual non-modal action. Blender passes the current [[Blender bContext Structure]] and [[Blender Operator Instance Structure]], giving the function access to active application state and the operation's RNA-backed settings.

The callback can retrieve values through [[Blender Operator RNA Properties]], call editor services, and delegate lower-level changes to the [[Blender BKE API]]. It returns an operator status such as finished so the handler system knows how to continue processing the event.

An optical see-through display combines a direct view of the physical world with generated light by means of an optical combiner. The user sees real objects through the display while virtual imagery is reflected or projected into the same line of sight.

Because the real view does not pass through a camera, it retains natural resolution and low visual delay. The virtual camera must be calibrated to the user's eye, and the system has limited control over real-world brightness, focus, and occlusion.

An optimal solution is a [[Feasible Solution]] whose objective value is no worse than that of every other feasible point.

A linear program may have one optimum, several tied optima, no feasible solution, or an unbounded objective. For a solvable linear program, at least one optimum occurs at a basic feasible extreme point.

An optimal stopping problem asks when to stop examining sequentially arriving options in order to maximize a reward or minimize a cost. Each decision must account for the danger of accepting too early and the danger of passing the best option.

The defining constraint is that rejected choices cannot later be recovered. The [[Secretary Problem]] gives a concrete strategy: reserve an initial sample for comparison, then accept the first later candidate that exceeds that benchmark.

An optional parameter declares a default value used when the caller omits that argument. Required parameters precede optional ones, making the minimum contract visible in the method signature.

A named argument associates a value with a parameter name at the call site. It improves clarity when several values share a type and can allow optional values to be supplied without listing every earlier default. Renaming a public parameter can therefore affect callers that use names.

An optional prop is a component input that the consumer may omit. In a TypeScript props interface, the optional marker distinguishes it from inputs every use of the component must supply.

The component must define behavior for the missing value. It may render nothing for that feature, select a [[Default Prop|default value]], or derive the behavior from other inputs.

An orbit camera revolves around a target while maintaining a radial distance. Its state is naturally stored with horizontal and vertical angles plus distance rather than as an unconstrained world position.

Those spherical parameters are converted into a camera position each update, and the camera looks back toward the target. Angle and distance limits prevent unwanted flips, clipping, or movement through the target.

An orbit is continuous [[Free Fall]] in which gravity bends motion around a central body. For a circular orbit, setting gravitational force equal to the required centripetal force gives $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/(GM)$. Higher circular orbits have lower speed but longer period.

An ordered classification rule belongs to a priority list of if-then conditions. Prediction tests rules in sequence and uses the consequent of the first antecedent satisfied by the observation.

Ordering resolves conflicts without combining every matching rule, but it makes a rule's meaning depend on all earlier entries. A default rule at the end supplies a class for cases that satisfy no learned condition.

An ordered integral domain has a total order compatible with addition and multiplication by positive elements. Its positive elements are closed under addition and multiplication.

Such a domain must have characteristic zero, because repeated positive copies of one cannot return to zero.

An ordered R script prefix uses leading numbers to communicate a project's intended execution sequence. Names such as `01-import.R` and `02-clean.R` make dependencies visible in a directory listing.

The ordering is documentation, not a substitute for explicit inputs and outputs between stages.

An ordinal feature takes values from a set with a meaningful order but without guaranteed numerical spacing. Educational degrees can be ordered from bachelor to master to doctorate, yet the gaps between those levels are not measurable as equal quantities.

Algorithms may exploit the ranking while avoiding arithmetic interpretations that the scale does not support. Treating an ordinal variable as either unordered categories or fully quantitative values discards or invents structure.

An organ-on-a-chip is a small engineered tissue model designed to reproduce selected structures and functions of an organ within a controlled device. Microfluidic flow and mechanical or biochemical inputs create conditions difficult to maintain in an ordinary culture dish.

The model is intentionally partial: it is useful when the reproduced function matches the biological question or therapy being tested.

An organoid is a three-dimensional tissue model produced when stem cells differentiate and self-organize into structures that reproduce selected features of an organ. Developmental programs create architecture rather than a printer placing every cell directly.

Organoids capture useful multicellular behavior but vary between samples and remain incomplete representations of mature whole organs.

An organoid-on-a-chip combines stem-cell self-organization with the controlled flow and stimulation of a microfluidic device. The organoid supplies complex tissue development, while the chip regulates transport and exposes measurable environmental conditions.

The integration can improve maturation and experimental control but inherits variability from organoids and interface complexity from microfluidics.

An oriented bounding box is a rectangular collision volume whose axes can rotate with the enclosed object. It usually fits a rotated model more closely than an [[Axis-Aligned Bounding Box]].

The improved fit makes intersection tests more expensive because overlap must be evaluated along candidate separating axes rather than by comparing world-axis intervals alone.

An orphaned verb is a [[Game Verb]] with little or no relationship to the rest of a game's interactive vocabulary. It may be used for one isolated action and then forgotten because other rules do not reinforce or develop it.

Orphaned verbs increase [[Cognitive Load]] without creating much depth. A design can avoid them by making its important verbs serve multiple purposes and interact with multiple objects, rather than adding a new control for every special case.

An orthogonal clustering view seeks a projection whose directions carry little or no overlap with those supporting a prior clustering. Clusters found in that projection emphasize variance hidden from the original view.

Geometric orthogonality provides a clear diversity criterion for numeric data, but it is stronger than semantic difference and may discard useful shared information. The new projection still requires an independent cohesion and stability assessment.

An orthogonal projection maps a point to the closest point in a specified linear subspace. The difference between the original and projected point is perpendicular to that subspace, which minimizes squared reconstruction distance.

Projecting samples onto selected basis directions produces lower-dimensional coordinates. In principal-component analysis, the chosen subspace maximizes retained variation and minimizes squared reconstruction error among linear subspaces of the same dimension.

An orthonormal basis consists of basis vectors that are mutually orthogonal and each have norm one.

Coordinates in such a basis are obtained directly through inner products. Arranging the basis vectors as matrix columns produces an [[Orthogonal Matrix]], which preserves lengths and simplifies projections, QR factorization, and diagonalization.

An outflow valve meters how quickly conditioned air leaves the pressure vessel and thereby regulates cabin pressure. Positive-pressure relief protects against excessive internal differential, negative-pressure relief prevents damaging external overpressure, and a dump valve rapidly releases cabin pressure when commanded. The valve system must coordinate rather than rely on the inflow source alone.

An outlier is an observation that deviates enough from other observations to suggest it may have arisen from a different mechanism. It can be an error, a rare valid case, or evidence of a distinct process.

Declaring a point anomalous requires an explicit reference context. Global distance, local density, statistical probability, and cluster membership can produce different judgments.

In life-science measurements, an outlier can arise from an undesired technical process such as scanner damage or amplification bias. The source demonstrates that one extreme value can severely distort the sample mean, variance, correlation, and t-test, motivating robust and rank-based alternatives.

An outline is a line drawn around an element for emphasis, often when the element has focus. Its style, width, and color resemble border components, and an offset can move it away from the border edge.

Unlike [[CSS Borders]], an outline occupies no layout space and need not follow a rectangular shape. It is an all-or-nothing decoration rather than four independently styled sides.

An output device is a physical device that communicates information from a computer to a user. It is also called a display and may stimulate vision, hearing, touch, smell, taste, or the sense of balance rather than only showing images.

The computer generates or models information and the output device converts it into a perceptible form. In a [[3D User Interface]], the choice of output device affects which [[Interaction Technique]]s are practical. Its [[Display Fidelity]], [[Latency]], resolution, ergonomics, and sensory coverage can all change task performance and [[User Experience]].

An overdetermined linear system has more equations than unknowns. Measurement data commonly produce such systems, and an exact solution may not exist.

A [[Least Squares Approximation]] chooses the vector whose predicted right-hand side is closest to the observed one, using a [[Normal Equation]], [[QR Decomposition]], or [[Singular Value Decomposition]].

An R data frame is a rectangular object whose columns represent variables and whose rows represent observations. Different columns may have different classes, while every column must align to the same set of rows.

Data frames are the principal R objects for health-data analysis. Analysts can select columns, subset rows, add recoded variables, pass the object into functions, and create revised copies as checkpoints. This object-centered workflow differs from the implicit row loop of the [[SAS Data Step]].

The life-science workflow in the source imports delimited tables as data frames and then uses dplyr operations to select variables and filter experimental groups. Row and column alignment makes the object a natural interface between raw observations, graphics, and statistical models.

The book treats the data frame as the main interface among imported records, cleaning operations, visualizations, and predictive models. Reviewing its dimensions, names, classes, and sample rows makes the transition from external resource to analytic object explicit.

An R function call applies a named operation to supplied arguments and returns a value, possibly with side effects such as drawing a plot. Named arguments can make intent clearer when a function accepts many options.

Calls can be nested, assigned to objects, or connected with an [[R Pipe Operator]], making them the basic compositional unit of R analysis.

An R function packages a sequence of operations behind a named interface and returns a result. Functions reduce duplication, clarify intent, and let the same logic operate on different data through arguments.

A well-designed function limits hidden dependencies and documents the inputs, output, and important side effects.

An R package is a distributable collection of functions, data, and documentation that extends base R. Packages let analysts assemble the capabilities required for a project instead of installing one monolithic statistical program with every possible component.

Published packages on CRAN follow documentation requirements and can be installed without licensing fees. Their flexibility creates a maintenance obligation, because a package may depend on other packages and may evolve independently of the R version used in production.

Installation and loading are separate operations: `install.packages` places a package on the system, while `library` attaches it to the current R session. This distinction lets an analysis declare the packages it uses without reinstalling them on every run.

The book further distinguishes installing a package from making it available in a session. [[R Library Attachment]] exposes exported functions on the search path, while an explicit [[R Package Namespace]] can identify the provider without attaching it.

An R package namespace identifies which package supplies a function or object. The `package::function` notation calls an exported function without attaching the whole package and makes name conflicts visible in code.

Explicit namespaces are particularly useful in reusable scripts and functions where several packages may export similarly named operations.

An R style convention is a consistent set of rules for names, files, spacing, comments, and layout. Consistency reduces the mental work of reading and reviewing code without changing its statistical meaning.

A project should adopt a documented style and apply it across scripts and reusable functions.

An R support function file is named after the principal function it defines when practical. Matching file and function names makes reusable logic easier to locate in a project.

Related small helpers may share a file when their grouping is clearer than one file per function.

An R-module M is flat exactly when Torᵢᴿ(N,M) vanishes for every R-module N and every positive degree i. It is enough to test the first obstruction in standard formulations.

The criterion turns preservation of all exact sequences into a homological vanishing condition. Nonzero Tor identifies where tensoring with M destroys injectivity.

An R-module M is p-primary when its set of associated primes is exactly {p}. Its zero divisors are therefore controlled by one [[Prime Ideal]].

For a Noetherian module, p-primary behavior can be characterized through injection into M_p together with annihilation of each element by some power of p. Primary modules are the quotient pieces arising from [[Primary Submodule]]s.

an RDS collection is a way to publish access to a single application or set of applications from within
the Remote Desktop Web Access portal.
Here is one perfect example of a use case for RemoteApp. A doctor’s office needs to allow its local
hospital to have access to one of its on-premises healthcare systems. This doctor’s office already has
an RDS farm, and we could simply provide hospital staff with logins and virtual sessions on that RDS
farm, but that would have given them access to double-click on any application installed on the RDSH
servers. It sounds better if we could restrict hospital staff to only run a single application. The answer?
Publish that lone application as a RemoteApp application inside a new RDS collection. These are the
bare steps to utilizing RemoteApp:
1. Create an RDS deployment; maybe you already have one.
2. Create a new RDS collection to keep these RemoteApp applications separate from your full
virtual sessions. It is possible to host both full desktop sessions and RemoteApp on the same
RDS collection and on the same RDSH servers, but Microsoft does not recommend it. Best to
keep them separated.
3. It usually makes sense to narrow the scope of this new collection so that only members of
a specific group have access. This way, you can easily restrict who has access to launch this
application.
4. Install the necessary application on your RDSH servers in the collection.
5. Publish a RemoteApp application inside your RDS collection properties.

An RNA enum property item describes one choice through an internal integer value, a unique identifier, an optional icon, a user-facing name, and a longer description. Arrays of these records define the options shared by the RNA, interface, and Python APIs.

Empty identifiers can represent menu separators, while a null identifier terminates the array. As part of a [[Blender RNA Typed Property]], the item list separates stable program values from the labels and explanations shown to users.

An RNA process item tells the `makesrna` generator which repository source file, optional API file, and definition function belong to a wrapped data family. The generator maintains an array of these items and calls each function to construct the corresponding RNA records.

This table is the build-time inventory behind [[Blender RNA Generated Source]]. By pairing source names with [[Blender RNA Definition API]] callbacks, it ensures each selected DNA type contributes its structures, properties, and accessors to the final [[Blender RNA System]].

An RNA refine function examines a general wrapped DNA record and returns the more specific [[Blender StructRNA]] that describes its runtime subtype. This is useful when several visible types share one underlying C structure but expose different subsets of fields.

Light data illustrates the pattern: a general light record can refine to point, area, spot, or sun descriptions. The function lets [[Blender PointerRNA]] retain one data address while the [[Blender RNA System]] selects the correct properties for access and presentation.

An RNA typed property extends the common [[Blender PropertyRNA]] layout with operations and metadata for a particular value kind. Boolean, integer, float, enum, pointer, collection, string, and other variants can supply scalar or array accessors, defaults, ranges, units, and update callbacks.

Generated property objects connect those descriptors to DNA fields through getter and setter functions. This makes the [[Blender RNA Access API]] type-safe at its boundary and lets the same property drive operator settings, interface controls, and Python attributes.

An RStudio project associates an analysis with a particular folder and opens R with that folder as its [[R Working Directory]]. Code, data, and supporting files can then use paths relative to a shared project root.

The source recommends projects as a simple organizational boundary for beginners. They reduce dependence on machine-specific absolute paths and help collaborators reproduce the same file relationships.

An S-polynomial combines two polynomials so that their leading terms cancel. Multipliers derived from the least common multiple of the leading monomials align those terms before subtraction.

S-polynomials expose conflicts between different possible reductions. [[Buchberger's Algorithm]] repeatedly reduces them; a generating set is a [[Gröbner Basis]] when all required S-polynomials reduce to zero.

An SDK-style Windows desktop project uses the compact `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WindowsDesktop` project format to build Windows Forms or WPF software on .NET Core 3. Properties select the executable type, target framework, language version, and the desktop UI framework used by the project.

Package and project references are declared explicitly in the project file, which makes the build inputs easier to inspect than older verbose formats. A successful conversion still requires testing because changing the project system can expose missing assemblies, unsupported APIs, or files that were previously copied implicitly.

The seven base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity, measured by the meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela. An ultrametric distance matrix records the tree-derived distance for every pair of leaves. Reordering its rows and columns consistently can reveal nested blocks: low within-cluster values collect near the diagonal and higher values separate larger branches.

The book demonstrates this with iris measurements, a Ward dendrogram, and the matrix read from that dendrogram. The matrix is more than a visualization aid: its ordered block structure is a numerical fingerprint of hierarchical relationships and can guide seriation of observations.

An ultrametric is a distance satisfying the strong triangle inequality: the distance from x to z is no greater than the larger of the distances from x to y and y to z. It is more restrictive than the ordinary triangle inequality.

For any three points, the two largest pairwise distances are equal. The corresponding triangle is equilateral or isosceles with a small base. This geometry is why nested cluster relationships can be represented by a rooted tree rather than by arbitrary overlap among neighborhoods.

An unbounded interval extends indefinitely in at least one direction on the [[Number Line]]. The inequality (x>-1) describes every real number to the right of (-1), while (x\leq2) extends without bound to the left.

An arrow shows the unbounded direction in a graph. The finite endpoint is open for a strict inequality and closed for an inclusive one. Infinity is not a real endpoint that can be included; it indicates that no finite boundary stops the interval.

An uncertainty density function assigns probabilities to the possible values of an imprecisely observed attribute or object. It preserves more information than a simple interval because likely and unlikely realizations are distinguished.

Classification algorithms can integrate a test, rule, or distance over this density. The result reflects expected behavior across possible values rather than pretending that a single point estimate was observed without error.

An unclassed choropleth maps each numeric value directly to a position on a continuous color scale. It preserves more of the variable's ordering than a [[Classed Choropleth]] and avoids artificial interval boundaries. However, viewers cannot reliably distinguish many fine color differences or recover exact values. The continuous legend must show the numeric range, and outliers can compress most regions into a narrow visual span.

An uncountable set cannot be placed in one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. Its members cannot all be exhausted by any infinite sequence indexed by natural numbers.

The real numbers are uncountable, and removing a [[Countable Set|countable subset]] from an uncountable set leaves an uncountable remainder. [[Cantor Diagonal Argument]] demonstrates this by constructing an element omitted from every proposed list.

An underdetermined linear system has fewer equations than unknowns. When consistent, it typically has infinitely many solutions because some variables remain free.

A [[Minimum-Norm Solution]] selects the solution closest to the origin. It can be expressed using a [[Pseudoinverse]] when the needed rank conditions hold.

An undirected graph has edges that can be traversed in either direction. An edge connecting vertices $A$ and $B$ therefore represents the same connection whether it is approached from $A$ or from $B$.

Reciprocal social relationships and two-way bridges can be modeled this way. When the direction of a relationship matters, the appropriate model is instead a [[Directed Graph]].

An unequal group power calculation allows comparison groups to have different sample sizes. One group's size may be fixed by disease prevalence, recruitment limits, or the available records while the calculation solves for the other.

Imbalance generally supplies less information than the same total sample divided evenly. Planning should therefore distinguish the number of available events from the total number of observations and avoid assuming that a large dataset automatically makes every subgroup comparison well powered.

An unintended consequence is an effect that arises outside the immediate purpose of an action. It often appears when a local fix participates in a larger or delayed [[Feedback Loop]] that was not considered.

A change may reduce a visible problem in the short term while strengthening the conditions that recreate it later. [[Systems Thinking]] helps reveal these effects by widening the boundary and timescale of analysis.

An unknown probability distribution marks a place where the model has not specified how plausibility is allocated across a variable's values. If that variable is always known evidence in every intended question, its prior factor may cancel during normalization and need not be supplied.

Otherwise the model must represent the available knowledge with an explicit form, such as a justified uniform distribution or a parameterized family. Calling the distribution unknown does not by itself define an inference.

An unknown variable is a [[Variable]] whose value is constrained by an equation or inequality and must be determined. In (3x-5=28), (x) is unknown because only particular values make the assertion true.

Solving transforms the relationship into an equivalent form that isolates the unknown. A symbol does not become an unknown merely by appearing in an expression; it may instead stand for an arbitrary parameter or a known quantity. Identifying the role of each symbol prevents a solution process from treating every letter as something to solve simultaneously.

An unmanned aerial vehicle carries no onboard human pilot. If it is not fully autonomous, it also depends on a ground controller and communication link; autonomous operation adds sensing, state estimation, mapping, planning, and feedback control. Mission suitability follows from the entire system rather than the airframe alone, including payload, battery, propulsion, and the environment to be observed.

An updateable game object exposes behavior that advances its state during the update phase of the [[Game Loop]]. Its update operation receives game delta time so movement, animation, and other temporal behavior can remain frame-rate independent.

The [[Game World Object Registry]] can iterate only the objects that require updates. An object that is purely visual or static does not need to implement this capability.

An upper triangular matrix is a [[Square Matrix]] whose entries below the main diagonal are zero. Its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries.

An upper triangular system can be solved by [[Back Substitution]]. In [[LU Decomposition]], the factor $U$ has this form, and [[QR Decomposition]] also produces an upper triangular factor.

An X-ray tube accelerates electrons through tens of kilovolts toward a metal target, commonly tungsten. Rapid deceleration produces a continuous bremsstrahlung spectrum, while inner-shell transitions add characteristic lines. Most electron energy becomes heat rather than X-rays, so target material, cooling, filtration, voltage, and current shape safe operation.

An X.509 certificate binds an asserted identity to a public key and includes a digital signature from its issuer. A TLS client validates the signature and certificate chain to decide whether the server's presented key belongs to the named endpoint.

The certificate exposes a public key rather than the server's private key. Trust therefore depends on the issuing authority, validity constraints, hostname relationship, and protection of the corresponding private key.

An xtable table converts supported R objects into LaTeX or HTML tabular markup with configurable formatting. It is useful for model summaries and tables that require more output control than a basic printer.

The generated markup should still be reviewed for meaningful labels and appropriate precision.

Analog computing represents a quantity through a continuously varying physical quantity, while digital computing represents it with discrete symbols. A mechanical cam shaped like an equation is analog; a numerical procedure executed with pulses is digital.

The categories were not sharply named until the 1930s and often coexisted in early systems. Digital methods prevailed because discrete states were easier to copy, control, and combine reliably at electronic speed.

Analog fire-control systems represented equations of motion directly through electrical or mechanical relationships. Continuously changing radar and tracking inputs adjusted a computed firing solution in real time.

These systems succeeded before general digital computers were practical. Their design raised lasting questions about feedback, automatic control, and how human operators should interact with fast machinery.

Collecting Player Information
For analog tabletop games and offline games where you have no access to the player’s behav-
ioral data, user behavior data is difficult to obtain and often of little use. However, most games
developed today have some form of online component or connection. Either the player is
directly connecting to a game server or the game is able to send anonymous information back
to a server for analysis. In addition, free-to-play (F2P) games yield and require a great deal more
information about the players’ behavior that helps you understand if the gameplay is balanced
and the game overall is healthy.
If the game can report back to a central server, then you can place calls in the game software
to record behavioral information. This information is recorded and typically sent back to the
server as a short string that identifies a player’s ID, where they are in the game when this infor-
mation is collected, and any other information you may need (such as how far the player is into
their current session).
It’s tempting to put analytics calls on everything, but this can do more harm than good.
Ultimately, you want to gather only the information that will help you create a more balanced,
engaging experience. The metrics you collect are often called key performance indicators (KPIs).
These are the numbers and metrics you watch to make sure your game is doing well, players are
enjoying it, and nothing is horribly out of balance. Another way to say this is that if something is
not a KPI, don’t bother collecting it: it becomes data you have to spend time analyzing that has
no real benefit.
When collecting user behavior data, you need to ensure that the information is recent and
is regularly collected. Not being able to access recently collected information or having it be
collected only sporadically does not help your understanding at all. If the information is more
than an hour or so out of date, it is often stale and not very useful. If it’s more than a day out of
date, it may lead you to make poor decisions about the game (unless you’re using it retrospec-
tively or, for example, to compare to the same day in the previous week for trends in behavior).
The ideal is continuous and near-real-time data collection: you should know what’s going on in
your game at any given moment. Realistically, this data may be collected only once every few
minutes, but that’s sufficient.
Grouping Players Together
The data you collect on a player is aggregated with data on other players into cohorts (or
groups) so that you can get an overview of how most players interact with the game. (With
only a few exceptions, individual player behavior information isn’t useful and can even lead
you astray.) One of the most common methods for creating player cohorts is to put all players

Getting Into the Game
Once players enter your game, you can record what they do next as they play the game. Recall
the example of Tumbleseed from Chapter 9. The game creators measured their players’ progress
and determined that most of them never made it to the first major checkpoint and that about
80% of the players who made it that far didn’t make it to the next milestone. Those are huge
losses, indicating that in some way the game is not balanced or engaging. Either the players
are finding the game boring or overwhelming. The remedies in each case are different, but the
underlying issue is the same and can be addressed only when you figure out why players come
in (clearly interested in the game) and the leave again soon after.
Measuring a player’s FTUE often includes their response to the game’s tutorial or opening
moments. Tutorials are meant to teach players how to navigate the game, and yet they are often
just frustrating and get in the player’s way. On the other hand, having no tutorial can mean throw-
ing the player into the game without their knowing what they’re doing, which can be equally con-
fusing and frustrating. Looking at how your players behave during the first few minutes of play
can help you balance this part of the game so that you keep as many players as possible playing.
Retention
In addition to keeping players playing, you want to keep them coming back. Retention is often
measured in terms of days. Day zero (D0) is the day someone first opens the game. D1 is the
next day. D7 is a week after they first started playing, and D30 is one month later. You can
group players into cohorts based on when they started playing and track their behavior from
there. What percentage come back on D1, D7, and D30? How can you improve this by improv-
ing their FTUE and by making sure they have in-game incentives to come back? For example,
many games (especially F2P games on mobile platforms) give the players bonuses or similar
if they come back the next day after they start playing. The game is very clear about this and
celebrates the player’s return—as well it should. A game that can’t bring players back the next
day is going to have a very difficult time succeeding.
Another aspect of tracking players’ playing behavior is to look at how the day-to-day numbers
of players changes. The number of individual players who play on any given day is called the
daily active users (DAU). This is sometimes referred to as a “heartbeat” number, as it can tell you
at a glance if the game is doing okay right now. DAU varies considerably by day of the week, so
seeing a drop-off on a Tuesday probably isn’t significant, as this is often the lightest gameplay

eCPU is effective cost per user—how much it costs on average to bring in a new player. So if the
average player plays your game for a year, and it costs $1 per month per player for the server,
bandwidth, upkeep for the development team, and so on, AND you ended up having to pay

back, averaged across all players, had better be more than $3 + $1 × 12, or $15. This means that
if, on average, across his or her entire lifetime, each player is paying you only $10, you’re essen-

analytics in this light.
All this talk about revenue and monetization may not be what you think of as game balance
or even game design. Monetization design is, however, increasingly part of game design. You
as a game designer have to be aware of and open to both design and analytical solutions to
creating a game that is commercially successful. This may mean selling a game online for a
single price, which is a more traditional approach, or putting it up for free with the opportunity
for players to choose to purchase in-game items if they want. Properly constructing the game
experience so that players do not feel that they must make purchases but that they can if they
wish and that they choose to do so enough to make the game successful is a key part of mon-

Usage
Aside from issues of bringing in players, keeping them playing, and encouraging them to make
purchases in the game, there are a variety of straightforward usage-based metrics you can col-
lect and analyze.
For example, if you have quests in your game, do they all get completed about the same
amount? If there is one that is done repeatedly, it might be unbalanced in the player’s favor. Or
if there is that almost no one completes, is it too difficult or tedious? You can also look at how
people die in the game or how they lose; are there aspects of the game that you wouldn’t see

ANATOMY AND COMPOSITION OF THE SKIN 165
A medium-sized organ, our skin spans an area covering approximately 1.6 to 1.9 sq. meters
(Rinzler, 2009) and accounts for approximately 15% of our overall body weight (Kanitakis, 2001).
We have two general types of skin— hairy and glabrous (naturally hairless)—both of which are
capable of a remarkably complex set of functions falling into three main categories: protection,
regulation, and sensation.
Protection— Located at the interface between the external environment and our internal
physiology, skin serves as a protective barrier against a variety of threats, including mechanical
impact and pressure (Sembulingam and Sembulingam, 2012), dangerous ultraviolet (UV)
radiation (Brenner and Hearing, 2008), and biological pathogens (Nestle et al., 2009).
Regulation— Our skin serves the vital role of regulating and stabilizing body temperature
through constriction and dilation of blood vessels (Charkoudian, 2003) and secretion and
evaporation of water.
Sensation— Also serving as the primary interface with our physical surroundings, our skin
contains an extensive network of nerve cells specifically designed to detect changes in
the environment as well as generate sensations we feel related to the properties of our physical
world with which we have contact. It is with these nerve cells that we are able to detect
the tactile and force feedback cues provided by such devices as a vibrating controller used for
navigating in, and manipulation of, augmented and virtual reality simulations.
Skin Layers
As detailed in Figure 9.1, human skin is composed of two primary layers, each of which varies
in thickness and function. The top, outermost layer is referred to as the epidermis (from the
Greek word epi, meaning “on top,” and derma, meaning “the skin”) (Oxford, 2015). This layer
serves as a physical and chemical barrier separating interior physiology and the external
environment (Madison, 2003; Denda, 2000). A dynamic structure, the epidermis is made of
tightly packed, scale-like cells that regenerate approximately every 45 days. The epidermis is
thinnest on the eyelids (.05 mm) and thickest on the palms and the soles of the feet (1.5 mm)
(NIH, 2006).
The second layer, known as the dermis, provides support for the epidermis and accounts for
approximately 80 percent of the thickness of the skin. The dermis is principally composed
of connective tissue (collagen) containing hair follicles, glands, blood vessels, nerves,
and sensory receptors. It gives the skin its elasticity and serves the structural purpose of
cushioning the body (Boundless, 2015). Also varying in thickness depending on location (1.5 to
4 mm), the dermis layer is highly vascular and contains more than 11 miles of blood vessels
(Jablonski, 2013). This venous network keeps the skin oxygenated and supplied with nutrients

Mechanoreceptors
As detailed in Figure 9.2, human skin contains four major types of receptors that respond
specifically to different types of mechanical stimulation resulting from physical interaction
with our surroundings: Meissner corpuscles, Merkel disks, Pacinian corpuscles, and Ruffini endings.
Known as mechanoreceptors, these sensors send information to our central nervous system
regarding touch, pressure, vibrations, and cutaneous tension (Purves et al., 2001). All four are
also categorized as low-threshold (or highly sensitive) receptors because each responds to weak
mechanical stimulation.

All mechanoreceptors function in the same basic manner:
1. An external stimulus or force acts on the surface of the skin.
2. The force is transferred deeper into the skin where it stimulates a mechanoreceptor.
3. The mechanoreceptor generates an action potential (electrical impulse).
4. The action potential is sent along afferent nerves to the central nervous system resulting in
a conscious perception, behavioral response, or both (Geffeney and Goodman, 2012).
Mechanoreceptor Classification
The four types of mechanoreceptors we will be exploring in this section are classified in two
different ways: by their rate of adaptation and by the size of their receptive fields.

Mechanoreceptor Details
All four main mechanoreceptors differ in physical size, geometry, range of sensitivity to
static and dynamic stimuli, location in the skin, population density, specific manner of
function, and more. With all of these features, it is important to remember that despite the
specificity of the descriptions, there is considerable overlap in the response of different
mechanoreceptors to a single stimulus event. As an example, the controller buzzing in your
hand as you manipulated an object within a virtual environment or the thump felt on your
chest coming from a gaming vest will elicit a response from several different receptors,
including those detecting deep pressure, cutaneous stretching, and vibration (which
translates into perception of texture).
Merkel Disks
A Merkel disk is a specialized sensory nerve ending characterized by a disk-shaped epithelial
cell attached to an afferent nerve fiber. Typically this nerve fiber is a branch of medium-to-large
diameter nerves serving a cluster of disks (Netter, 2013). As shown in Figure 9.6, Merkel disks
are generally located in skin layers at the boundary between the epidermis and the dermis and
are found in the greatest numbers within glabrous skin in such locations as beneath the ridges
forming our fingerprints (Bear et al., 2007, p 389). When the appropriate stimulus is present,
deformation of the disk wall opens ion channels in the nerve fiber. The influx of sodium (Na +)
ions results in action potential firing (Maksimovic et al., 2014).

Response Characteristics
Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting (RA) and respond to the onset and removal of the
mechanical stimulus. They are particularly efficient in transducing information when textured
objects are moved across the skin (Purves et al., 2001; Burgess, 2012), the slippage of objects
(Barker and Cicchetti, 2012), as well as shape changes in exploratory and discriminatory touch
(Mancall and Brock, 2011). Meissner corpuscles respond maximally to mid-range frequencies (20–50
Hz) (Gilman, 2002) such as might be produced from a smooth cotton shirt (Klein and Thorne, 2006).
Pacinian Corpuscles
A Pacinian corpuscle (alternatively known as a Lamellar corpuscle) is characterized by an
oval-shaped geometry and is composed of several dozen concentric lamellae (thin layers) made
of fibrous connective tissue separated by layers of fluid. The entire corpuscle is encased on the
outside by collagen. At the center of the corpuscle is a cavity containing one or more afferent
nerve fibers (Purves et al., 2001).
When physical pressure from an external force acts on the corpuscle and causes a deformation
of the structure, the nerve fiber at the center is also bent or stretched, opening ion channels
(chemical gates) into the outer membrane and allowing the influx of sodium ions. The greater
the external force, the greater the deformation of the corpuscle and the larger the influx of
sodium ions, resulting in the generation of an action potential within the afferent nerve fiber
that is forwarded to the central nervous system.
The largest of the four major types of mechanoreceptors, Pacinian corpuscles are also the
fewest in number (Kandel, 2000). As shown in Figure 9.8, Pacinian corpuscles are located deep
in the dermis layer of the skin and even within the subcutaneous fat.

Muscle Spindles
Muscle spindles are small, elongated sensory organs enclosed within a capsule and are found in
nearly all skeletal muscles of the human body (Purves et al., 2001). As is obvious from Figure 9.11,
a muscle spindle derives its name from actual geometry and structure. The concentration of
spindles varies depending on specific muscle function, with higher counts found in muscles
involved with delicate movements (Taylor, 2006).

Similar to Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles, the main body of a muscle spindle is composed
of a capsule of collagen. Within this capsule and oriented parallel to the regular muscle
fibers are specialized intrafusal muscle fibers, around which is wound an afferent nerve ending
(dendrite) known as an annulospiral ending.
When regular muscle fibers stretch, tension in the intrafusal fibers increases, opening ion
gates and stimulating the annulospiral nerve ending. This results in the generation of an
action potential. The greater the tension, the greater the frequency of impulses fired off. These
impulses quickly reach the central nervous system, and a return signal is sent to control the
extent to which the muscle is allowed to stretch and, in doing so, prevent damage (Prochazka,
1980; Sherwood, 2015).
Golgi Tendon Organs
Unlike muscle spindles, which measure stretch, another sensory receptor, the Golgi tendon
organ, measures tension in tendons (the tough, fibrous material connecting muscles to bone).
When you lift an object, be it a baseball or heavy weight, or a limb is acted on by an external
force, Golgi tendon organs tell you how much tension is being exerted by the muscle. From the
viewpoint of a force feedback device such as those discussed in Chapter 10, Golgi tendon organs
are the sensors that tell you how much force is being imparted to your hand or other limbs.

exclusive and OR for bool types. When applied, it computes both operands and

Null coalescing
(??)
The null coalescing operator computes both operands and returns the operand that is
not null. It's used like so: int y = x ?? 1;. In this scenario, if x is null, y is
assigned a value of 1; otherwise, y is assigned a value of x.

The risks – cache coherency, performance issues, and false
sharing
However, risks are involved and things can and do go wrong. One risk is to do with what’s termed
cache coherency, and the other is often termed false sharing; the following sections delve into them.
What is the cache coherency problem?
Let’s first understand the key notion of cache coherency. Multicore SMP systems have two or more CPU
cores, each with its own private internal caches (and Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLBs)). The
caches typically follow an optimized read-ahead, write-behind policy (with respect to main memory,
RAM). This means, of course, that data can be read into the CPU caches in a read-ahead manner (as
we just learned, reads and writes actually work in an atomic unit of a cacheline, not a single byte. So
the read-ahead performed is to optimize likely subsequent fetches, taking advantage of the principles
of both spatial and temporal locality of reference, which in turn simply means that “memory worked
upon recently is likely to be worked upon again in the near future,” both in terms of space (spatial
locality) and time (temporal locality)).
What about writes to memory? They’re governed via a cache writeback policy. When a data item (a vari -
able in your program) is modified (written to), it’s worked upon within the internal caches of the local
core and not flushed to (the possible unified cache and) the main memory (RAM) until a later point
in time, again optimizing performance; this is the so-called write-behind policy in action (as opposed
to a write-through policy where it’s immediately flushed).
We’ll take a simple example. Take a multicore SMP system with 2 cores (again, like the one concep -
tually shown in Figure 13.4). Say there’s a global integer N in RAM with the value 55. Now, at time t0.1
(see Table 13.3), let’s say a thread running on core #0 wants to modify it to a value – say, 41; we now
understand how it will work internally. Assuming there are CPU caches as shown in Figure 13.4 (L1,
L2, and shared L3), the value of N (55) is first read from RAM (across the buses) into the L3 cache (time
t0.2) and into core 0’s local internal (L1, L2) caches (time t0.3).

Computational devices
Now that we know we can have an arbitrarily large number of computational devices as
nodes in our network, it bears further scrutiny to discern what exactly a computational
device is. While this may seem obvious, at least initially, we can quickly identify where it
becomes unclear by way of an example.
As per our definition of a network, the device I'm using to draft this book right now might
well qualify as a self-contained network. I have a keyboard, mouse, monitors, and
computer, all connected by standardized channels of communication. This looks awfully
network-like at a conceptual level, but intuitively, we would be inclined to say that it is a
network of one, and so, not really a network at all. However, while the what of the non-
network status of my computer seems obvious, the why might be less clear.
This is where we benefit from clearly explicating what constitutes a computational device
for the purposes of our definition of a network. Simply being able to perform computation
is insufficient for a network node. In my example, I can tell you that my mouse (a relatively
high-end gaming mouse) certainly performs a number of complex calculations
transforming a laser-sensor signal into directional inputs to pass to my computer. My
monitors certainly have to do a fair amount of computation to transform the raw binary
data of pixel color values into the rendered screens I see 60 or 120 times per second. Both of
these devices are connected by way of reliable, standardized communication protocols to
my machine, but I wouldn't necessarily be inclined to consider them nodes on a network.
My computer, when connected to the internet, or my local home network, surely
constitutes a node, but its individual peripherals? I'm inclined to say no.

applies image processing techniques to the buffers, and the third pass composes the final
result from the individual buffers by sweeping over the buffers in depth order.

don’t want the full change to happen all at once. Instead, you need to

To create the appearance of continuous change, the updates need to
be made faster than the human eye can detect the individual
changes. Just like the difference between a slideshow and a film, the
secret to creating moving pictures is to change the graphic fre‐
quently, but only a little bit each time.
The accepted standard for “continuous” anima‐
tion on the web is 60 frames per second (fps), or
about 16ms betweeen updates. But this is only a
rough approximation.
If the updates from one frame to the next are
subtle, you can get away with a lower frame rate
(that is, longer time between updates) and it will
still look continuous. However, if the updates
involve significant changes—like moving long
distances across the screen—even 60fps can look
jumpy. You may need to soften the change with
a motion blur effect, to create the appearance of
smooth motion.
Continuous scripted animations therefore require repeated code
that runs at regular intervals, updating values a little bit at each iter‐
ation. That means we need two things:
• an animation update function that will keep track of all the in-
progress animations, and calculate and apply the current values
based on the current time
• a timer function that will call our update function at regular
intervals
Together, these create our animation loop.
The animation update functions can be as simple or as creative as
you like. We’ll give some basic examples, but we can’t cover all the
possibilities. But the timer functions are what drive your custom

(providing it is purely decorative), or embedded images. So the pos‐
sibilities are as open-ended as SVG itself.

But <pattern> elements are also complex in less inspiring ways. The
options for scaling the pattern tiles are so open-ended that they are
often confusing. And there are a few unfortunate details in the spec‐
ifications—and bugs in the implementations—which introduce
obstacles for many designs.
The next few sections outline some of the most common structures
for SVG patterns.
All the Units to Use
A <pattern>, like a gradient, can be scaled to the object bounding
box or to the user-space coordinate system. However, it is more
complicated than that. You have two attributes to set the scale:
patternUnits and patternContentUnits.
The patternUnits attribute sets the scale you use for defining the
size and position of the initial pattern tile. In other words, it controls
the attributes on the <pattern> itself. It defaults to
objectBoundingBox units.
The pattern tile attributes affected by
patternUnits are x, y, width, and height. Set
these attributes to percentages or numbers from
0–1 for objectBoundingBox units, or use any
SVG lengths if you change patternUnits to
userSpaceOnUse.
The patternContentUnits attribute sets the scale of the drawing
content inside the <pattern> element. It defaults to userSpaceOnUse
units. You can change it to objectBoundingBox units, or you can use
a viewBox attribute to define your own scale for each pattern tile. If a
viewBox is provided, patternContentUnits has no effect.
Avoid percentages in the pattern contents when
using a viewBox or objectBoundingBox content
units—they are not relative to the tile size, the
viewBox, or the bounding box.
Instead, the definition of 100% from the user-
space coordinate system is scaled up propor‐
tional to the scaling effect on all other units—
which is not particularly useful.
